title: Joins
summary: Combine orders, customers and coffees with INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN, find rows without a match, emulate the FULL OUTER JOIN MySQL lacks, avoid the accidental cross product and use MySQL's.
introduction: Orders store a customer_id and a coffee_id rather than names and prices; that is what keeps the data consistent when a name changes. A JOIN puts the pieces back together for a report. This lesson joins two and three tables, uses LEFT JOIN to keep customers who have never ordered, shows the one join MySQL does not have, and ends with a MySQL extension that lets UPDATE and DELETE use joins too. The rows are the ones loaded in the CRUD lesson.
learningObjectives: Join two and three tables with INNER JOIN and table aliases
Keep unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN and find them with IS NULL
Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN, which MySQL lacks, with UNION
Run a multi-table UPDATE safely inside a transaction

blocks.text: `JOIN ... ON` pairs each order with the customer whose `id` equals the order's `customer_id`. Rows with no partner on either side are dropped, which is why it is called an *inner* join; `JOIN` and `INNER JOIN` are the same thing. Short aliases (`orders o`) keep the column references readable, and `ORDER BY` is still needed, because a join does not promise any row order.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.quantity, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.content:
+----+---------------+----------+-----------+
| id | name          | quantity | status    |
+----+---------------+----------+-----------+
|  1 | Priya Nair    |        2 | shipped   |
|  2 | Priya Nair    |        1 | shipped   |
|  3 | Tomás Ribeiro |        3 | paid      |
|  4 | Mei Chen      |        2 | pending   |
|  5 | Yusuf Demir   |        1 | cancelled |
|  6 | Tomás Ribeiro |        2 | paid      |
|  7 | Priya Nair    |        1 | pending   |
+----+---------------+----------+-----------+
7 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: Each extra table gets its own `JOIN ... ON`. Both `customers` and `coffees` have a `name` column, so every reference must be qualified with its alias, and aliases on the output columns keep the report readable. Multiplying a `DECIMAL(6,2)` price by an integer quantity gives an exact decimal line total.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, k.name AS coffee,
       o.quantity, k.price * o.quantity AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN coffees k ON k.id = o.coffee_id
ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.content:
+----+---------------+----------------+----------+------------+
| id | customer      | coffee         | quantity | line_total |
+----+---------------+----------------+----------+------------+
|  1 | Priya Nair    | Morning Blend  |        2 |      25.00 |
|  2 | Priya Nair    | Yirgacheffe    |        1 |      16.00 |
|  3 | Tomás Ribeiro | Espresso Roast |        3 |      42.00 |
|  4 | Mei Chen      | Yirgacheffe    |        2 |      32.00 |
|  5 | Yusuf Demir   | Morning Blend  |        1 |      12.50 |
|  6 | Tomás Ribeiro | Decaf Colombia |        2 |      27.50 |
|  7 | Priya Nair    | Espresso Roast |        1 |      14.00 |
+----+---------------+----------------+----------+------------+
7 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: When the joined columns share a name on both sides you can write `JOIN coffees USING (coffee_id)` instead of `ON`. Our tables use `id` on one side and `coffee_id` on the other, so `ON` is required; it is also the form that works everywhere.

An inner join hides Hannah, who has never ordered. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table and fills the right-hand columns with NULL when nothing matches, which is what a report of *all customers* needs:

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

blocks.content:
+---------------+----------+
| name          | order_id |
+---------------+----------+
| Priya Nair    |        1 |
| Priya Nair    |        2 |
| Priya Nair    |        7 |
| Tomás Ribeiro |        3 |
| Tomás Ribeiro |        6 |
| Mei Chen      |        4 |
| Yusuf Demir   |        5 |
| Hannah Weiss  |     NULL |
+---------------+----------+
8 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: Testing that NULL is the standard way to find rows *without* a match. The same shape answers "which coffees have never been ordered?" by swapping the tables.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

blocks.title: A WHERE on the right table turns a LEFT JOIN back into an inner join
blocks.text: `LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.status = 'paid'` drops Hannah again: her `o.status` is NULL, and NULL fails every comparison. Conditions on the optional table belong in the `ON` clause, as in `ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'`, which keeps every customer and attaches only paid orders.
`RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image and keeps every row of the right table. Almost everyone writes outer joins as `LEFT JOIN` with the table to keep on the left, so you will rarely see it.

PostgreSQL and recent SQLite have `FULL OUTER JOIN`, which keeps unmatched rows from both sides. MySQL does not: `UNION` a `LEFT JOIN` with a `RIGHT JOIN` instead. `UNION` removes duplicate rows, so the matched pairs appear once; because every order here has a customer, the result equals the LEFT JOIN above, only sorted by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
UNION
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY name, order_id;

blocks.content:
+---------------+----------+
| name          | order_id |
+---------------+----------+
| Hannah Weiss  |     NULL |
| Mei Chen      |        4 |
| Priya Nair    |        1 |
| Priya Nair    |        2 |
| Priya Nair    |        7 |
| Tomás Ribeiro |        3 |
| Tomás Ribeiro |        6 |
| Yusuf Demir   |        5 |
+---------------+----------+
8 rows in set (0.00 sec)

blocks.text: MySQL accepts a `JOIN` without `ON` and treats it as a `CROSS JOIN`: every order paired with every customer, 7 × 5 = 35 rows. The symptom is a report with too many rows and inflated totals, never an error message.

blocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders JOIN customers;

blocks.text: MySQL lets `UPDATE` and `DELETE` join tables, so you can change orders based on a column of the customer. The statement below cancels pending orders from customers in Taipei. It is wrapped in a transaction and rolled back at the end, so the sample data is unchanged afterwards; the [Transactions lesson](/tutorials/mysql/transactions) explains the mechanism.

blocks.content:
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

Query OK, 1 row affected (0.01 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

+----+-----------+
| id | status    |
+----+-----------+
|  4 | cancelled |
+----+-----------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

blocks.text: The matching `DELETE` names the table to delete from before `FROM`: `DELETE o FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.city = 'Taipei';`. PostgreSQL spells the same idea `UPDATE ... FROM` and `DELETE ... USING`, and SQLite needs a subquery, so these statements are the first thing to rewrite when a project changes database.

questions.question: Which join lists every coffee, including those that have never been ordered?
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table (coffees) and fills the order columns with NULL when no order matches.
options: `coffees k JOIN orders o ON o.coffee_id = k.id`
`coffees k LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.coffee_id = k.id`
`orders o LEFT JOIN coffees k ON k.id = o.coffee_id`

questions.question: Leaving out the ON clause of a JOIN is a syntax error in MySQL.
questions.explanation: MySQL silently treats it as a CROSS JOIN and returns every combination of rows, which is why an unexpected row count is the only symptom.
